overview: This file combines a December 1947 State Department transmittal with a substantial August 1947 occupation-era report on civil transportation in Japan and a March 1949 internal policy memorandum. The report describes the organization and mission of the Civil Transportation Section of GHQ, SCAP, then assesses the condition, capacity, traffic, ownership, finances, and rehabilitation needs of Japan’s railways, merchant marine, highways, motor vehicles, and municipal transit. It uses numerous statistical charts to compare prewar, wartime, and early postwar conditions and advocates a coordinated transportation plan suited to Japan’s geography, resources, population, economy, and occupation requirements. The concluding memorandum records continuing U.S. policy uncertainty over Japanese civil aviation and shipping, including a stalemate before the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of report on civil transportation in Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits five copies of the Civil Transportation Section’s August 1947 report on the organization and operation of Japan’s transportation system.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 1464 encloses a report entitled “Civil Transportation in Japan,” prepared by the Civil Transportation Section of GHQ, SCAP. It explains that the report outlines the section’s organization and describes the current operation of Japanese transportation. Filing and preparation notations identify the document under decimal file 894.70.

subfiles.title: Civil Transportation in Japan
subfiles.from: Civil Transportation Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Surveys Japan’s postwar rail, water, highway, and municipal transportation systems and sets out the organization and planning objectives of the occupation’s Civil Transportation Section.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the wartime deterioration of Japanese transportation and the supervisory institutions established during the Allied occupation, including the Civil Transportation Section and the Shipping Control Authority for Japan. Detailed statistical discussions cover railway traffic and labor, merchant-fleet losses and reparations, coastwise and foreign shipping, deficient highways, motor-vehicle production, buses, tramways, subways, and other municipal services. It identifies shortages of coal, gasoline, tires, repair parts, raw materials, and investment incentives, while criticizing deficits, surplus labor, government control, and poorly coordinated rates. The final section argues for a balanced system responsive to Japan’s mountainous geography, concentrated population, dependence on foreign trade, changing labor relations, and possible growth in motor transport and private enterprise.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on transport and communications policy in Japan
subfiles.from: H. F. Amrine, Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: M. W. Bishop, Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends acknowledging U.S. civil-aviation objectives in the forthcoming Japan policy statement while noting that a coherent shipping-policy statement is not yet possible.
subfiles.summary: Amrine reports that U.S. civil-aviation proposals for Japan are stalled and unlikely to become acceptable to the Far Eastern Commission for several weeks. He nevertheless recommends that the new policy statement mention U.S. civil-aviation objectives and the government’s nearly three years of work on the issue; the suggested text was attached but is not present in the OCR bundle. He adds that shipping policy remains too unsettled for a coherent statement, although Department specialists expect to address it once German shipping policy is nearly complete, and he anticipates discussions with Mr. Saugstad and his staff.

interest: The principal report is a valuable quantitative snapshot of Japanese transportation less than two years after surrender, preserving occupation officials’ assessments of infrastructure, traffic, labor, fleet composition, costs, and material shortages across several transport modes. It is also revealing as an ideological document: its authors repeatedly connect technical rehabilitation to private enterprise, reduced government control, economic stabilization, and the broader political objectives of the occupation. The 1949 memorandum is especially useful when read beside the report because it shows that, despite extensive technical analysis, U.S. policy on Japanese aviation and shipping remained unresolved at the diplomatic level.
